headline: Presidential hopefuls focus on cost and corruption this Thanksgiving
author: Alec Dent

paragraphs.text: Holiday weeks tend to be slower for political news, with political arguments moving from the national stage to family dinner tables. But the next presidential campaign cycle still carried on this Thanksgiving, albeit at a bit slower pace.
Here’s what likely 2028 candidates were up to this week between eating turkey and watching football:
Thanksgiving messages focused on rising costs
A number of Democrats considered likely to run for the presidency in 2028 released statements on Thanksgiving emphasizing how expensive life has become for Americans.

As the midterm elections demonstrated, cost of living is top of mind for voters, and an American Farm Bureau Federation survey this month found the average cost of a Thanksgiving meal for 10 people increased by 6 percent from last year.

“It’s Thanksgiving week. The only spending I enjoy is time with family. These high prices for feeding everyone come from the Iran war, the trade war, and the reckless deficit. Needless to say, I am not grateful for those things,” Sen. Rand Paul (R-Kentucky) said in a social media post.

“Everything from the turkey to the flight home is more expensive this Thanksgiving under Trump, and families are feeling the squeeze,” Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker (D) posted. “Thanksgiving dinner costs rose up to 11% in 2026, with 121,000 fewer Americans expected to travel thanks record fuel costs and soaring airfares.”

“American families are hurting this year. Thanksgiving dinner costs 6% more than last year. Gas is up 17%,” Rep. Ro Khanna (D-California) said on X. Khanna called for ending the war with Iran, Medicare-for-all, a $25 minimum wage and making “data centers pay” to address rising costs.
“A turkey costs 10% more than last year. A flight is 22% more. Gas is around $4. Trump keeps lining his pockets while you search yours to make ends meet,” said Sen. Cory Booker (D-New Jersey).
Jensen Huang scandal framed as a corruption issue

Nvidia rehired Jensen Huang as its CEO Monday after President Donald Trump personally intervened on his behalf, prompting criticism from Democrats and Republicans alike about Trump’s unusual role in the decision. Trump has substantial investments in Nvidia and has long been fond of Huang, who was CEO of Nvidia when it made a $25 million pledge to Trump’s ballroom project.
Likely presidential contenders entered the debate about Huang’s return this week and many were focused on potential corruption in the process.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) called Huang’s return “another example of the dangerous combination governing this country: a rigged system that protects those at the very top no matter what, and a corrupt White House that cannot be trusted to put the economic well-being and safety of American families first.”

“You want to know why people are angry? Because they look at this and they say, ‘If you’re rich and powerful and you’re friends with the president, you can get away with everything,’” former New Jersey governor Chris Christie said in an interview with CNBC.
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) accused the billionaire class of trying to play by different rules in an interview with the Axios Show.
“The thing that makes people so angry about this is it seems like it’s rules for thee, but not for me,” Moore said. “Frankly, if that was any of us, we would be held to a different type of standard.”
Khanna also called for “fairness,” saying that “Rules should apply to everyone. That’s why I took on the Epstein class.”
“The rich & powerful, like Jensen, do not get to evade export controls or accountability just because it props up the stock price,” Khanna said.

Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Arizona) told MS NOW that the case was about “billionaires protecting other billionaires” and Trump “protecting his billionaire friend who gave $10 million or more, millions of dollars, to his ballroom project.”
“If something like this would have happened to someone in the Navy or our military, you wouldn’t get a call from the president,” said Kelly, a Naval veteran. “You would get a call from the FBI.”
Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Michigan) suggested that Trump’s financial stake in Nvidia could have influenced how his administration approached oversight of the company.

“When President Trump came to power, he made the decision, kind of a shocking decision, to allow our most sophisticated AI chips, made by Nvidia, to be sold to the Chinese government, to Chinese companies,” Slotkin said. “Unsurprisingly, we know now, that he has made tremendous money in Nvidia stock because of that decision.”

Focusing on potential corruption in this high-profile incident makes a lot of sense: corruption was one of voters’ top concerns in the midterms and helped propel Democrats to major victories across the country.
The DNC revealed its 2028 debate schedule

The Democratic National Committee said on Monday that it will host a dozen presidential primary debates in the 2028 cycle, with the first scheduled for June 2027. Five debates will take place in 2027, with seven scheduled for 2028.

Also notable: The DNC is requiring debate participants to denounce super PAC spending on their behalf, agree not to participate in unsanctioned debates and skip campaigning in states that disregard the DNC primary calendar. (The latter is significant as the DNC has officially named South Carolina as the first state in its primary calendar, even though New Hampshire state law requires it to hold the nation’s first primary.)
Other 2028 stories from this week

• Vice President JD Vance stopped by Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio on Wednesday with his family to serve lunch to service members ahead of visiting with family in Vance’s home state for Thanksgiving.

• Trump set his sights on California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D), a likely 2028 candidate, during a speech at the Justice Department on Monday. Trump criticized Newsom’s effort to commute all death sentences in the California penal system, and accused Newsom of having more sympathy for killers on death row than for victims and their families.

• Pritzker announced that his state will not participate in the new federal school voucher program set to launch in January, saying the program would “siphon money from public schools for private education.”Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) responded by saying the program will not “‘siphon’ money from public schools; the money is in addition to any state funding.”Former Virginia governor Glenn Youngkin (R) accused Pritzker of siding “with the unions over kids.”
• Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-Texas) called for their state to be the home of a Space Force training academy.

• Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Kentucky) suggested Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth should be removed from office over the Army’s detonation of nearly 10,000 pounds of degrading lead explosives in Iowa. Massie led a failed effort to impeach Hegseth for his role in the Iran war earlier this month.
